opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time it felt like a pretty big moment for me, even though from the outside it might look like just a professor changing schools. I had been in contact with Professor Tu, and I was really excited about the idea of working with him, so when I heard he was moving to UCSD, my first reaction was a bit of uncertainty. When you're a young student, you've built your plans around a particular person and a particular place, and suddenly the ground shifts a little.

But looking back, I think it turned out to be a very lucky thing. UCSD was a really good environment. It's in San Diego, the weather is wonderful, the atmosphere is relaxed, and the computer vision and machine learning community there was growing. Because Professor Tu was starting fresh in a new place, the group was small at the beginning, and that meant I got a lot of direct time with him. It wasn't a big, established lab where you're one of many students and you mostly talk to senior PhDs. It was more like we were building something together.

Professor Tu also has a very particular style. He's very independent in his thinking, he doesn't just chase whatever is popular, and he cares a lot about whether an idea is fundamentally interesting. Being close to him in that early stage of his time at UCSD really shaped how I think about research: try to find problems that are simple but important, and don't be afraid to go a different direction from everyone else.

So if you ask how I felt, at first it was a mix of surprise and some anxiety, but in hindsight I'm very grateful. A lot of things in life are like that. You can't really plan them perfectly, and sometimes the change you didn't expect ends up being the best thing that could have happened.

r001.rationale: The response does not say Professor Tu prepared Xie for the move or downplayed UCSD’s likely ranking; it describes Xie’s uncertainty and later appreciation of UCSD.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn as Saining Xie, drawing only on the conversation history.

Honestly, it felt like the ground shifting under me a bit. I had just started my PhD at UCSD with Professor Tu, and then he told me he was leaving. He actually gave me a choice, which I'm grateful for. One option was to stay at UCSD, and the other was to follow him. For a student in the first year, that's a pretty big decision, because you don't really have a research identity yet, and your advisor is basically your whole world.

I ended up choosing to follow him. Looking back, I think it was the right call. The most important thing in a PhD is the person you learn from, not the campus. Professor Tu was very hands-on, he cared a lot about how you think about a problem, and that kind of mentorship isn't something you can easily replace. So even though the move was disruptive at the time, it probably shaped the way I do research more than anything else in those years.
